title: Health and science passages: claims, numbers, cause and effect
blurb: Read health and science passages exactly: match every number to its group, follow cause and effect, and separate what was found from what was proved.
question: A HESI A2 passage reports that children's bicycle head injuries in a county fell from 120 to 70 after a helmet law, while the county also built new bike lanes. One option says the law cut head injuries in half. Another says head injuries fell as helmet use rose. Which is supported, and why is the other wrong twice over?

teach.body: Formally, a health or science passage presents claims supported by evidence: measurements, study results and explanations of how one thing leads to another. In plain English, these passages are packed with numbers, causes and careful qualifiers such as 'may', 'about' and 'tend to'. HESI A2 items test whether you read them exactly: which number belongs to which group (a supporting detail) and what the evidence actually supports (a conclusion).

(1) In 2019, Lake County passed a law requiring bicycle riders under 16 to wear helmets. Observers at county parks found that helmet use among child riders rose from 35 percent before the law to 80 percent two years later.

(2) Emergency room visits for bicycle head injuries among children fell from 120 in 2018 to 70 in 2021. Visits for children's bicycle arm and leg injuries stayed at about 300 a year. Officials credit the helmet law, but they note that the county also built 12 miles of protected bike lanes in 2020.

head: Number
What it measures
When
teach.caption: Most wrong options move a real number to the wrong group, unit or year.

teach.body: Before you answer, pin each number to its group, its unit and its time. Watch three slips: a count read as a percent, a change read as a final value ('fell by 50' versus 'fell to 50'), and a rough size word that overstates. A drop from 120 to 70 is 50 visits, about 42 percent: 'nearly half' is close, 'cut in half' is not. A rise from 35 to 80 percent is 45 percentage points.

rows.label: Lake County
values: Head injuries fell as helmet use rose
The law cut head injuries in half

teach.caption: The passage names a second change (bike lanes), so it cannot prove the law was the cause.

items: Tag each number with its group, unit and year as you read.
Find the cause-and-effect claims and their signals: because, so, led to, as a result.
Note every qualifier: may, about, some, tend to, suggests.
Look for other changes at the same time and for any comparison group.
Choose the option that matches the numbers exactly and claims no more than the qualifiers allow.

teach.caption: Head injuries fell while arm and leg injuries held steady: crashes did not simply become rarer.

teach.text: Three science-passage traps: (1) a number moved to the wrong group or year (80 percent is helmet use, not injuries); (2) two things that happened together turned into proof of cause, especially when the passage names another change; (3) a qualifier dropped, so 'may lower' becomes 'lowers' and 'some' becomes 'all'.

teach.h: Scenario: Andre weighs the helmet passage
teach.body: Andre Thompson, applying to a respiratory therapy program, gets 'Which conclusion is best supported?' on the Lake County passage. He rejects 'The helmet law cut children's head injuries in half': 120 to 70 is about a 42 percent drop, and the bike lanes arrived in the same period. He notices that arm and leg injuries held steady, so children were not simply crashing less. He chooses 'Children's head injuries fell as helmet use rose,' which matches every number and claims no proven cause.

items: Pin every number to its group, unit and time before you answer.
A change ('fell by') is not a final value ('fell to'); percentage points are not percent.
Signal words show cause and effect: because, so, led to, as a result.
Two things happening together do not prove cause, especially when another change is named.
The best conclusion keeps the passage's qualifiers: may, about, some, tend to.

summary: You can now read health and science passages precisely, matching each number to its group and time and following the passage's cause-and-effect chain. You can choose the conclusion the evidence supports and reject options that move numbers, drop qualifiers or turn a correlation into proof.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) In January, observers at Westbrook Hospital watched staff on four units and recorded whether they cleaned their hands before entering a patient's room. Hand hygiene was observed 58 percent of the time.

(2) The hospital then placed sanitizer dispensers inside every doorway and posted each unit's monthly rate at the nurses' station. By June, the rate had risen to 84 percent on three of the four units. On the fourth unit, where dispensers were installed late in May, the rate was 63 percent.

According to the passage, what was the June hand hygiene rate on the unit where dispensers were installed late?
options: 84 percent
58 percent
63 percent
26 percent
A.why: Paragraph 2 says that on the fourth unit, where dispensers arrived late in May, the June rate was 63 percent.

whyNot.0: Wrong group: 84 percent is the June rate on the other three units.
whyNot.1: Wrong time: 58 percent is the January rate across all four units.
whyNot.3: This is the gain on the three units (84 - 58 = 26 points), not a rate for any unit.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) A call center gave 200 employees desks that can be raised for standing. After three months, employees who stood at their desks at least two hours a day reported less lower-back pain than before, while those who rarely stood reported no change.

(2) Employees chose for themselves how often to stand. During the same three months, the company also began offering weekly stretching classes.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: Standing desks cure lower-back pain in office workers.
Frequent standers reported less back pain than before.
The stretching classes caused the drop in back pain.
Most employees stood at their desks two hours a day.
A.why: The passage reports that employees who stood at least two hours a day reported less back pain. Restating that finding is supported; claiming a cause is not, because workers chose how often to stand and stretching classes began at the same time.

whyNot.0: Overreach: one workplace's reports over three months cannot show that desks cure back pain.
whyNot.2: The classes are a possible other cause, but the passage gives no evidence that they caused the drop.
whyNot.3: Unsupported: the passage does not say how many employees stood that often.

A.q:
Read the passage.

(1) When the body overheats, it sweats. As sweat evaporates from the skin, it carries heat away. In humid air, sweat evaporates more slowly, so the body cools less efficiently even though a person may be dripping with sweat.

(2) For this reason, weather services report a heat index, which combines air temperature and humidity into a single 'feels like' number. A 90°F day with high humidity can produce a heat index above 100°F.

According to the passage, why does the body cool less efficiently in humid air?
options: The body makes less sweat when the air is humid.
The heat index raises the temperature of the air.
Humid air holds more heat than dry air does.
Sweat evaporates slowly and carries off less heat.
A.why: Paragraph 1 states the chain: in humid air, sweat evaporates more slowly, 'so the body cools less efficiently.'

whyNot.0: Contradicts paragraph 1, which says a person may be dripping with sweat in humid air.
whyNot.1: Reversal: the heat index is a measure that describes how hot it feels; it does not change the air temperature.
whyNot.2: Outside knowledge: the passage explains the effect through slow evaporation, not through how much heat the air holds.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) A county offered free flu shots at eight elementary schools. Of the 3,200 students at those schools, 1,600 received the vaccine, compared with about 900 the year before, when shots were offered only at clinics.

(2) That winter, absences for flu-like illness at the eight schools fell by about a quarter. At nearby schools that did not host clinics, those absences stayed about the same.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: Flu absences fell at the eight schools but not at nearby schools.
Most students at the eight schools were vaccinated that year.
School clinics ended flu outbreaks at the eight schools.
Vaccinations nearly tripled after the school clinics began.
B.why: Paragraph 2 reports a drop of about a quarter at the eight schools and little change at nearby schools. The conclusion combines both facts and claims no more.

whyNot.1: Number slip: 1,600 of 3,200 is half, not most.
whyNot.2: Overstatement: absences fell by about a quarter; flu did not stop.
whyNot.3: Number slip: about 900 to 1,600 is less than double, not nearly triple.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) A school district measured carbon dioxide in 40 classrooms. Levels above 1,000 parts per million, a sign of poor ventilation, were found in 22 of them, most in the district's oldest building.

(2) After new fans were installed in the oldest building, the district tested again. This time, 4 classrooms were above 1,000 parts per million.

According to the passage, how many classrooms were above 1,000 parts per million before the new fans were installed?
B.why: Paragraph 1 says levels above 1,000 parts per million were found in 22 of the 40 classrooms, before the fans.

whyNot.0: 40 is the number of classrooms tested, not the number above the level.
whyNot.2: 18 is the improvement (22 - 4), not a count of classrooms above the level.
whyNot.3: 4 is the count after the fans were installed.

B.q:
Read the passage.

(1) When a town switched its streetlights to bright white LED lamps, residents on several blocks complained that light shone into their bedrooms at night.

(2) Light at night can delay the release of melatonin, a hormone that helps signal the body that it is time to sleep. The town has since added shields that aim the light downward on those blocks.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: LED streetlights cause sleeplessness in most of the town's residents.
The shields keep melatonin from being released during the night.
The town responded to concern that the lights could disturb sleep.
Residents on every block asked the town to remove the new lights.
B.why: Residents complained of light in their bedrooms, the passage explains that night light can delay melatonin, and the town added shields on those blocks. Together these support a response to a possible effect on sleep.

whyNot.0: Overreach: the passage says night light can delay melatonin; it gives no evidence about most residents' sleep.
whyNot.1: Reversal: the shields reduce light in bedrooms, which would help, not block, melatonin release.
whyNot.3: Overstatement: complaints came from several blocks, and the passage describes complaints about light in bedrooms, not requests to remove the lights.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Two neighboring towns had similar rates of emergency room visits for childhood asthma. In 2021, Ashford replaced its diesel school buses with electric ones; Brookline kept its diesel fleet.

(2) Over the next two years, asthma-related emergency visits by school-age children fell 18 percent in Ashford and 5 percent in Brookline. Both towns had a mild pollen season in 2022.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: The electric buses ended childhood asthma attacks in Ashford.
Children in Brookline had more severe asthma than in Ashford.
The mild pollen season fully explains Ashford's larger drop.
The bus change may help explain Ashford's larger decline.
C.why: The towns started out similar, both had a mild pollen season, and only Ashford changed its buses; its visits fell more. That pattern supports the modest claim that the bus change may help explain the difference.

whyNot.0: Overstatement: visits fell 18 percent; asthma attacks did not end.
whyNot.1: Unsupported: the towns had similar rates at the start, and the passage does not compare severity.
whyNot.2: Both towns had the mild season, so it cannot explain why Ashford's drop was larger.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) In 2015, 20 percent of adults in Mill County reported that they smoked. By 2023, the figure was 12 percent.

(2) Health officials point to a 2017 tax increase on cigarettes and to free quit-smoking classes that began in 2019.

According to the passage, how did the share of adults who reported smoking change from 2015 to 2023?
options: It fell by 12 percentage points.
It fell by 40 percentage points.
It fell by 8 percentage points.
It fell by 60 percent overall.
C.why: The share went from 20 percent to 12 percent: 20 - 12 = 8 percentage points.

whyNot.0: 12 percent is the 2023 value, not the size of the change.
whyNot.1: Mixes units: the drop is 40 percent of the starting share (8 of 20), but only 8 percentage points.
whyNot.3: 60 percent is the share that remained (12 of 20), not the size of the drop.

C.q:
Read the passage.

(1) Some shoppers believe that the word 'natural' on a food label means the food is healthier.

(2) In the United States, however, the FDA has no formal definition of 'natural' for most foods. Its long-standing policy is that the word means nothing artificial or synthetic has been added. A 'natural' snack can still be high in sugar, salt or fat.

Which conclusion would the author most likely agree with?
options: A 'natural' label by itself does not show that a food is healthy.
Foods labeled 'natural' are healthier than similar foods.
The FDA should ban the word 'natural' from food labels.
Foods labeled 'natural' contain little sugar, salt or fat.
C.why: The author reports the shoppers' belief and then answers it: the word means nothing artificial was added, and a 'natural' snack can still be high in sugar, salt or fat.

whyNot.1: This is the shoppers' belief that the author reports in paragraph 1 and then disputes.
whyNot.2: Advice the author does not give; the passage explains the label, it does not call for a ban.
whyNot.3: Contradicts paragraph 2, which says a 'natural' snack can be high in sugar, salt or fat.

reteach.title: The rooster and the sunrise
reteach.question: Every morning a rooster crows, and a few minutes later the sun comes up. Does the rooster make the sun rise? How does that question help with HESI A2 science passages?

blocks.h: Together is not the same as because
blocks.body: The rooster crows before every sunrise, so the two always go together, yet nobody thinks the rooster causes the dawn. Science passages are full of pairs like this: a new program and a drop in injuries, more sleep and better grades. The passage shows that they happened together. Unless it rules out other causes, the safe conclusion keeps a qualifier: the change 'went along with' or 'may help explain' the result.

blocks.text: When a passage names a second change in the same period, or no comparison group, an option that says 'caused' or 'proves' is almost certainly the trap.

explain.h: Match the number to its group
explain.body: Every number in a science passage belongs to one group, one unit and one time. Detail questions often offer the right number for the wrong group, so check all three before you answer.

test.q:
Read the passage.

(1) A clinic tracked flu shots for two age groups last fall. Among patients 65 and older, 72 percent were vaccinated; among patients 18 to 64, 41 percent were.

(2) The clinic's goal is to vaccinate at least 70 percent of the patients in each adult age group.

According to the passage, which group met the clinic's goal?
options: Patients 18 to 64
Patients 65 and older
Both age groups
Neither age group
test.why: The goal is at least 70 percent. Patients 65 and older reached 72 percent; patients 18 to 64 reached 41 percent.

whyNot.0: Patients 18 to 64 reached 41 percent, well below the 70 percent goal.
whyNot.2: Only the older group reached 70 percent; the younger group did not.
whyNot.3: Patients 65 and older reached 72 percent, which meets the goal.

explain.body: Science passages often explain why something happens in a chain: A leads to B, and B leads to C. Signal words (because, so, as a result, can) mark each link. A 'why' question is answered by the link just before the effect, not by a later effect.

test.q:
Read the passage.

Smoke from wildfires hundreds of miles away drifted over the city, raising the level of fine particles in the air. Because these tiny particles can irritate the airways, the health department advised people with asthma to stay indoors, and pharmacies reported a rise in inhaler refills that week.

According to the passage, why did the health department advise people with asthma to stay indoors?
options: Fine particles in the air can irritate the airways.
Pharmacies were running short of inhaler refills.
The wildfires were burning close to the city limits.
Heat from the fires had raised the city's temperature.
test.why: The passage links the advice directly to its cause with 'because': the tiny particles can irritate the airways.

whyNot.1: Reversal: the rise in refills is reported alongside the advice, not as its cause, and no shortage is mentioned.
whyNot.2: Contradicts the passage: the fires were hundreds of miles away.
whyNot.3: Outside idea: the passage does not mention heat or temperature.

explain.body: A survey or study that finds two things together (an association) does not show that one causes the other, especially when the groups differ in other ways. The supported conclusion restates the association; the trap claims a cause.

test.q:
Read the passage.

A survey of 1,500 college students found that those who slept fewer than six hours a night reported lower grade point averages than those who slept seven or more hours. Students who slept less also reported working more hours at paid jobs.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: Short sleep causes lower grades in college students.
Long hours at paid jobs are the real cause of lower grades.
Most college students sleep fewer than six hours a night.
In the survey, shorter sleep went with lower reported grades.
test.why: The survey found shorter sleep and lower reported grades together. Because the short sleepers also worked more, the passage cannot show which factor, if either, caused the lower grades.

whyNot.0: Causal overreach: the passage reports an association, and work hours are a second difference between the groups.
whyNot.1: Also causal overreach: work hours are another possible factor, but the passage does not show they are the cause.
whyNot.2: Unsupported: the passage does not say what share of students slept under six hours.

explain.body: Science writers choose words such as 'may', 'some', 'early research suggests' and 'results have varied' on purpose. The correct option keeps that strength. An option that removes the qualifier, or flips it into the opposite certainty, overstates the passage.

test.q:
Read the passage.

Early research suggests that regular stretching may reduce muscle soreness after exercise for some people. Results have varied from study to study, and researchers say larger studies are needed before firm advice can be given.

Which statement best reflects the passage?
options: Stretching prevents muscle soreness in most people who exercise.
Stretching may ease soreness, but the findings so far are mixed.
Research has proved that stretching does not reduce soreness.
Stretching reduces soreness more than rest does after exercise.
test.why: The passage says stretching 'may' reduce soreness 'for some people' and that results have varied. This option keeps both qualifiers.

whyNot.0: Drops the qualifiers: 'may' and 'some people' become 'prevents' and 'most people'.
whyNot.2: Flips the claim into the opposite certainty; the passage says results are mixed, not that stretching fails.
whyNot.3: Unsupported comparison: the passage does not compare stretching with rest.
